sheet-1.description: Sheet 1 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood shows the business centre of the borough along Haddon Avenue, which runs across the sheet from left to right, at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. Above Haddon Avenue the sheet takes in the lower ends of the blocks between Crestmont, Madison, Knight and Harvard Avenues, filled with frame dwellings and a few small automobile buildings, and a compass rose at the left. A dash-dot match line lettered A and B crosses this upper area and joins sheet 5. Haddon Avenue itself is lined by a row of brick and frame stores on its south side east of Knight Avenue (drugs, shoes, a grocery and a fish store, numbered 608 to 630), with a fire alarm box and a telegraph or telephone hydrant marked on the street. South of Haddon Avenue the blocks hold paired brick dwellings with a repeated plan, frame dwellings, and the plant of John J. McCloskey, manufacturer of textile machinery, with its machine shop, storage and a long spur from the railroad. A garage for twenty cars with concrete floor stands near Knight Avenue. The lower part of the sheet is crossed by the tracks of the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (Pennsylvania Railroad) in a wide corridor, below which South Atlantic Avenue and Park Avenue run parallel to Haddon Avenue with a row of numbered detached houses on the block between them. Four, six, nine and twelve inch water pipes are drawn in the streets. The bottom of the sheet is blank and refers to sheet 21; the neighbouring blocks are on sheets 5, 2 and 26.
notes: Crestmont Avenue is Crestmont Terrace today; Gorman Avenue south of Haddon Avenue is West Gorman Avenue.
Madison Avenue and Knight Avenue are East Madison Avenue and East Knight Avenue north of Haddon Avenue and West Madison Avenue and West Knight Avenue south of it.
The streets are offset where they cross Haddon Avenue; the printed names do not change.
Only the junctions along Haddon Avenue could be used as control, so the sheet is placed from points on a single street.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-2.description: Sheet 2 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers the middle of the Haddon Avenue business district, from Harvard Avenue at the left to Collings Avenue at the right, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. Haddon Avenue crosses the sheet from side to side. North of it, between Spring Street and Haddon Avenue, lie blocks 32, 33 and 39 of frame dwellings, St. Paul's Lutheran Church, and, at the right, two rows of paired brick dwellings flanking Lincoln Avenue and a row of brick stores numbered 701 to 721 fronting Haddon Avenue. South of Haddon Avenue the frontage is mixed: a wallpaper and office building, a battery station, Duff's Collingswood Garage with space for 35 cars, auto repair shops, and a row of stores and a drug store at the Collings Avenue diagonal. Collings Avenue runs from the upper right corner of the sheet southwest across the tracks as a diagonal street; on it stand the Borough Hall, the volunteer fire department with a descriptive note on its apparatus, the General Water Supply Company, and the premises of Richard Frech. Robert C. Taylor's lumber yard with a coal trestle and cement bins lies against the railroad. The West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (Pennsylvania Railroad) crosses the lower third in a wide corridor with freight and passenger sheds and a platform. South of it are Atlantic Avenue and South Atlantic Avenue, Park Avenue, Lakeview Drive, a triangular block drawn with the diagonal of Collings Avenue, a small plot marked Knight Park, and blocks of detached dwellings and apartments. Water pipes of four to twelve inches are drawn in the streets. Adjoining sheets are 1 at the left, 3 at the right, 6 above and 21 below.
notes: Woodlawn Terrace north of Haddon Avenue is Woodlawn Avenue today; Spring is Spring Avenue.
Collings Avenue north of Haddon Avenue is East Collings Avenue in OpenStreetMap; the diagonal stretch to the southwest is Collings Avenue.
The junction of Atlantic Avenue, Collings Avenue and Lakeview Drive is an open triangle with pipes drawn through it and was left out of the control.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-3.description: Sheet 3 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood shows the eastern half of the Haddon Avenue business district, from Collings Avenue at the left to Fern Avenue at the right, at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. Haddon Avenue crosses the sheet and is lined on both sides by brick and frame stores, the densest commercial frontage in the borough. On the north side, between Collings and Washington Avenues, stand a row of stores numbered 723 to 749, the Collingswood Garage for 30 cars, a vacant old church and a block of dwellings; east of Washington Avenue are the stores numbered 801 to 817, the Collingswood National Bank, the Public Library, Fisher and Richards Floral Company with its greenhouses, and the Collingswood Theatre for moving pictures with a long note on its fireproof construction. On the south side are the post office, hardware, grocery and meat stores, a bakery, Public School No. 1, the Masonic Hall, drug stores and a telephone exchange. Behind them lie the Collingswood Coal and Supply Company and lumber piles. South of the blocks the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (Pennsylvania Railroad) crosses the sheet in a wide corridor with Railroad Avenue on its north side, and J. H. Van Meter's garage for 55 cars stands at the tracks. South of the railroad are Atlantic Avenue and Park Avenue with blocks 44 and 47 of detached dwellings on either side of Dayton Avenue, and Lees Avenue at the right. Two compass roses and the number of the adjoining sheets are printed in the margins; sheets 2, 4, 7, 8 and 22 adjoin.
notes: Irving Avenue is Irvin Avenue today; Collings Avenue north of Haddon Avenue is East Collings Avenue.
Railroad Avenue north of the tracks is North Atlantic Avenue in OpenStreetMap; Atlantic Avenue south of the tracks is Atlantic Avenue.
Frazer Avenue and Haddon Avenue junction was not detected and no hand-picked point was added.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-4.description: Sheet 4 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers the eastern end of the Haddon Avenue district, between Fern Avenue and Lees Avenue at the left and the edge of the borough's built-up streets at the right, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. The top third of the sheet is blank above Haddon Avenue except for the compass rose, the title cartouche and the sheet number, and the lower end of the blocks above Haddon Avenue is bounded by the lines of the neighbouring sheet 8. Haddon Avenue crosses the sheet with a row of frame dwellings along its south side, between the Fern Avenue and Bellson Avenue corners and again between West Stiles Avenue and the right edge, some with undertaker, office and auto garage uses at the left. Behind them, in block 22, stands the coal and feed yard of C. P. Mohrfield with its elevator, open bins and a spur from the railroad, and block 189 holds dwellings between Bellson and West Stiles Avenues. The tracks of the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (Pennsylvania Railroad) cross the lower part of the sheet in a wide corridor, with a watch house at Lees Avenue. South of the railroad, South Atlantic Avenue and Park Avenue enclose blocks that are mostly vacant, with St. John's Roman Catholic Church and School at the left on Lees Avenue and, at the right, a row of detached dwellings on Dill Avenue and block 151. Several streets are cut off at the sheet edges by lines marking where sheets 3, 8, 22 and 23 take over. Water pipes of four, six and eight inches and fire alarm boxes are drawn in the streets.
notes: Bellson Avenue is Billson Avenue today; West Stiles Avenue and East Stiles Avenue are the same names in OpenStreetMap.
South Atlantic Avenue is Atlantic Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
North Atlantic Avenue (the street along the north side of the tracks, not lettered on this sheet) was left out: its two junctions here lay 4.7 and 5.5 m off the drawn position.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-5.description: Sheet 5 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers two rows of residential blocks in the north part of the borough, between Highland Avenue at the top and the rear lines of the lots facing Haddon Avenue at the bottom, which are drawn on sheet 1. From west to east the sheet is crossed by Crestmont Avenue at the left edge, Madison Avenue, Knight Avenue and Harvard Avenue at the right edge; Maple Avenue runs across the middle of the sheet parallel to Highland Avenue. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left, so the street grid stands square on the page although it runs about 23 degrees off true north on the ground. The blocks, numbered 103, 104, 106, 26, 27 and 288 among others, are filled with detached frame dwellings of two to two and a half stories, most set back on deep narrow lots, with frame and concrete-block private garages and a few coops and sheds along the rear lot lines. A handful of dwellings are of brick or have brick or stucco veneer, and a small building near Crestmont Avenue is drawn in blue as a stone or concrete structure. No commercial, industrial or institutional buildings appear on the sheet. Water pipes of four, six and eight inches are drawn in the streets, with fire hydrants and a fire alarm box at Crestmont and Highland Avenues. House numbers run along each frontage. The area above Highland Avenue is left blank and refers to sheet 9; sheet 26 adjoins on the left, sheet 6 on the right and sheet 1 below.
notes: Crestmont Avenue is Crestmont Terrace today; Madison Avenue and Knight Avenue north of Haddon Avenue are East Madison Avenue and East Knight Avenue.
Map, 50 ft. Highland to the rear of Haddon Av lots; Crestmont (Crestmont Terrace), Madison (East Madison), Knight (East Knight), Harvard Avs, Maple Av. One part. Pilot sheet.

sheet-6.description: Sheet 6 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers a residential district north of Haddon Avenue, from Harvard Avenue at the left to Collings Avenue at the right and from Highland Avenue at the top to Spring at the bottom, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. Three tiers of rectangular blocks stand between Harvard Avenue and Lincoln Avenue, separated by Highland Avenue, Maple Avenue, Summer and Spring and crossed by Woodlawn Terrace; they are numbered 29B, 30, 31 and 32 and are filled with detached frame dwellings of two to two and a half stories on deep lots, with scattered auto garages and coops, and one pink brick dwelling in each tier. In the upper right the street grid turns: Woodlawn Avenue and Lincoln Avenue run as parallel diagonals toward the north-east, Autumn Avenue cuts across them at an angle, and the long narrow lots between them, in blocks 38B and others, carry dwellings, poultry houses, coops and an auto house with a cement floor. At the far right the diagonal of Collings Avenue is lined with a long wagon shed and auto buildings. A dash-dot match line lettered A and B crosses the upper right and joins sheet 28. Along Lincoln Avenue and Collings Avenue, at the lower right, two rows of paired brick dwellings with a repeated plan occupy block 39. The compass rose and the title cartouche are printed in the upper margin and a scale of feet at the foot. Water pipes of four and eight inches are drawn in the streets. Adjoining sheets are 5 at the left, 2 below and 7 at the right.
notes: Woodlawn Terrace and Woodlawn Avenue keep their names in OpenStreetMap; the Highland Avenue junction at the diagonal Woodlawn Avenue is a junction with Woodlawn Avenue, not Woodlawn Terrace.
Spring is Spring Avenue today; Collings Avenue is East Collings Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
The junction of Maple Avenue and Collings Avenue was not detected.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-7.description: Sheet 7 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers a residential district north of Haddon Avenue between Collings Avenue at the left and Fern Avenue at the right, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. Maple Avenue crosses the lower part of the sheet and Lincoln Avenue and New Jersey Avenue run as diagonals in the upper half, so that the blocks at the top are cut at an angle, while the main grid below is formed by Washington Avenue and Frazer Avenue running down the page. The blocks, numbered 39A, 40, 41 and 42 among others, are filled with detached frame dwellings, some of brick or stucco, with garages and coops on the rear lines; several lots along New Jersey Avenue carry pink brick dwellings. The First Baptist Church, drawn in blue as a stone or concrete building, stands on the north side of Maple Avenue at Frazer Avenue, and a blue building at the left edge is drawn near Collings Avenue. At the lower left two rows of paired brick dwellings with their numbers (34 to 48) face Collings Avenue, and a diagonal lot line crosses the block above them. Maple Avenue jogs where it crosses Frazer Avenue, and its right-hand stretch lies farther down the page than its left-hand one. The compass rose and the cartouche are printed in the margins. Adjoining sheets are 6 at the left, 3 below, 8 at the right and 28 above, whose border is shown by a dash-dot line.
notes: Collings Avenue is East Collings Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
Maple Avenue jogs at Frazer Avenue; the modern node there was not detected and is not used.
Only five junctions were used as control; the fit has a leave-one-out error of 3.5 m.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-8.description: Sheet 8 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers the north-east part of the borough between Fern Avenue at the left and Homestead Avenue at the right, from Oriental Avenue at the top to Haddon Avenue at the bottom, drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. The sheet joins two street patterns. In the upper left, Fern Avenue, Lawnside Avenue and Oriental Avenue run on a diagonal, and the long narrow blocks between them (111, 112 and 42) are lined with detached frame dwellings set along the diagonal streets. To the right and below, the blocks follow the main grid between Maple Avenue, East Stiles Avenue and Homestead Avenue (blocks 113, 24 and 23B), with frame dwellings, a few of brick, and small garages and coops. The Collingswood Presbyterian Church, drawn in blue, stands on Maple Avenue at the left, and the Holy Trinity Protestant Episcopal Church faces Haddon Avenue in the lower left corner. Along Haddon Avenue at the foot of the sheet are frame dwellings and a few shops on the north side. The upper right is partly blank, with the compass rose, the cartouche and the sheet number, and a stepped boundary line where sheet 10 begins. Water pipes and fire hydrants are drawn in the streets and a fire alarm box at the foot. Adjoining sheets are 7 at the left, 3 and 4 below and 24 at the right.
notes: Homestead Avenue is East Homestead Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
The junctions of East Stiles Avenue and East Homestead Avenue with Haddon Avenue lie on the bottom edge of the image and were not detected.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-9.description: Sheet 9 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers the northern edge of the borough, a tall strip of mostly undeveloped blocks running north from Highland Avenue, which is the street along the bottom of the sheet. Crestmont, Madison, Knight and Harvard Avenues cross the part from bottom to top; the first three are narrow 50 foot streets and Harvard Avenue forms the right-hand side. The bottom blocks, numbered 173, 174 and 28A, carry rows of detached frame dwellings of two to two and a half stories, with a few brick or stucco dwellings in pink and a concrete-block garage in blue, set on deep narrow lots whose lot lines are drawn right up to the heavy block outlines. Farther north the same blocks are laid out in lots but hold few buildings; a short row of brick dwellings faces Crestmont Avenue, and a cluster of larger buildings stands in the upper right corner next to the sheet number. A public alley crosses the part from left to right about two thirds of the way up. The upper left is cut by a heavy zigzag line beyond which the sheet is blank and refers to sheet 27; sheet 26 adjoins on the left, sheet 28 on the right and sheet 5 below, where Highland Avenue is shared. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left, so the street grid stands square on the page although it runs about 23 degrees off true north on the ground. A compass rose and the Sanborn scale bar are printed on the sheet, and 4 and 8 inch water pipes with hydrants are marked along the streets.
notes: Crestmont Avenue is Crestmont Terrace today; Madison Avenue and Knight Avenue north of Haddon Avenue are East Madison Avenue and East Knight Avenue.
The public alley is Crestmont Lane in OpenStreetMap; its two junctions with Crestmont Terrace and East Madison Avenue were hand-picked.
Only the junctions along Highland Avenue and the alley give control, so the part is fitted from two rows of points and is a medium confidence placement.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-10.description: Sheet 10 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood shows a block of the borough along its eastern boundary with Haddon Township, where the street grid is turned almost a third of a circle from the northern part of town. Lincoln Avenue runs diagonally across the top of the part, with Center Street running down from it at the left; New Jersey, Fern and Lawnside Avenues run across the page, and Oriental Avenue runs down the left side of the lower blocks. Laurel Street leaves Lincoln Avenue at the upper right and continues south as a 20 foot alley. The blocks, numbered 35B, 35C, 42 and 111A among others, are filled with detached frame dwellings of two to two and a half stories on narrow lots; the long rows of near-identical houses along New Jersey, Fern and Lawnside Avenues are drawn with open porches, and the Lawnside Avenue row at the bottom is shown in pink as brick. A few dwellings near Center Street and Lincoln Avenue are also brick. At the right the part is bounded by the Borough of Collingswood and Haddon Township line, which runs beside a private lane. The upper left and the area left of Oriental Avenue are blank and belong to sheets 28 and 8; sheet 24 adjoins below. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with a compass rose in the upper right, and its grid is rotated so that north points toward the upper right rather than the upper left as on the northern sheets. Water pipes and hydrants are marked in the streets.
notes: The street lettered Center on this sheet is Center Avenue today.
Laurel Street is Laurel Avenue today; its junction with Lincoln Avenue is an offset crossing with a 20 foot alley to the south and was hand-picked.
The sheet is turned: the street grid fits at about +33 degrees rather than the -22 degrees of the northern sheets.
The private lane along the borough line is probably Burrwood Avenue; it was not used for control.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-11.description: Sheet 11 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood shows three rows of residential blocks in the northwest part of the borough, between White Horse Pike along the top of the sheet and Comley Avenue along the bottom. Richey Avenue and Cattel Avenue cross the sheet between them. McGill Avenue runs down the left side and Grant Avenue down the right, so the sheet holds two columns of streets and six street junctions. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned on the page: north points toward the left, so the lettering of the side streets reads sideways, and the compass rose stands in the left margin. The blocks, numbered 6, 7, 12 and 19, are lined with detached frame dwellings of two to two and a half stories on narrow deep lots, with house numbers in the 400 and 700 and 800 ranges. Several pairs of three-story frame semi-detached houses with a party wall face White Horse Pike. Rear lots carry private garages marked Auto, coops, storehouses and a long greenhouse behind the Pike frontage. A few dwellings are brick or stucco, and two small buildings are drawn in blue as concrete block. A vacant store is lettered on the corner of Richey and Grant. Water pipes of four and six inches are drawn in the streets, with test hydrants marked and the street widths of 60 and 70 feet. The empty blocks outlined on the left and right edges belong to sheets 18, 29, 12 and 13, which adjoin; no one of them is drawn here.
notes: McGill Avenue is Magill Avenue in OpenStreetMap, and Cattel Avenue is Cattell Avenue.
The sheet lies in West Collingswood, then part of Haddon Township, and its adjoining sheets are numbered 18, 29, 12 and 13 on the printed margins.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-12.description: Sheet 12 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers the centre of West Collingswood, four blocks wide and three deep, between White Horse Pike at the top and Comley Avenue at the bottom. Richey Avenue and Cattel Avenue cross it, and Grant Avenue, Collings Avenue and Eldridge Avenue run from the left edge to the right. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the left, so the street grid stands square on the page. This is the commercial part of the area. A row of two-story brick and frame stores faces the south side of Richey Avenue beside the Moving Picture Theatre, a drug store, a barber and tailor, a hall and a post office, and the post office sits on the next lot. On the opposite block are the Memorial National Bank, the Branch Library and St. Lukes Evangelical Lutheran Church in blue, with the West Collingswood M.E. Church near White Horse Pike. Smaller trades include a canvas goods factory with an electric motor, a hardware and paint store, a battery station and a paint shop. Christ P.E. Church, stone with a hot-air heating plant, stands on Comley Avenue. A row of brick stores is lettered wall paper, meats, confectionery and groceries, with dwellings above them. Dwellings fill the rest, with garages and coops behind, and a compass rose stands on the northeast block. Four-inch water pipes run in all the streets, and a fire alarm box is marked at several corners.
notes: Cattel Avenue is Cattell Avenue today.
Stores and institutions named on the sheet include West Collingswood M.E. Church, Memorial National Bank, Branch Library, St. Lukes Evangelical Lutheran Church and Christ P.E. Church.
The adjoining sheets named in the margins are 11, 15, 20 and 14.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-13.description: Sheet 13 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood shows three blocks of residential streets in West Collingswood at the western edge of the borough, between Comley Avenue at the top and the Atlantic City Railroad at the bottom. McGill Avenue runs down the left side and Grant Avenue down the right, and Taylor Avenue and Sloan Avenue cross the sheet. Champion Avenue appears at the bottom as a diagonal street running beside the railroad. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the left of the page, and the compass rose stands on the left margin. The blocks, numbered 13, 18 and 19, are mostly detached frame dwellings of two to two and a half stories with their private garages, coops and storehouses. A large pink building at the northwest corner of the upper block is lettered as heated by steam and lit by electricity. A paint shop and an auto shop stand at the bottom of the lower block, and a printing shop and a carpenter shop are drawn beside Grant Avenue in the middle block. At the lower left corner there is a pair of brick dwellings. At the bottom right the drawn boundary of the Borough of Collingswood against the City of Camden crosses the sheet, with the tracks of the Atlantic City Railroad of the Philadelphia and Reading Railway fanning out beyond it. Water pipes of four and six inches are marked in the streets, with fire alarm boxes and hydrants at several corners. The large blank areas on both sides are the neighbouring sheets 11, 14, 29 and 30.
notes: McGill Avenue is Magill Avenue in OpenStreetMap; Champion Avenue still exists beside the rail line, but its modern junctions are not used as control because it is drawn wide and diagonal.
The Atlantic City Railroad is lettered with P. & R. Ry beside it.
Adjoining sheets named in the margins are 11, 14, 29 and 30.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-14.description: Sheet 14 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers four blocks of West Collingswood between Comley Avenue at the top and Champion Avenue and the Atlantic City Railroad at the bottom. Grant Avenue forms the left edge of the blocks, Collings Avenue passes through the middle, and Eldridge Avenue forms the right edge, with Taylor Avenue crossing between the upper and lower rows. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch and turned so that north points to the left, with the compass rose in the upper right corner. The blocks, numbered 14, 15, 16 and 17, are filled with detached frame dwellings of two to two and a half stories, garages and coops. A volunteer fire department stands on Collings Avenue near the lower corner of block 15 with a bell tower and a pool room; the legend lists one chief, one assistant and a number of men, an Anderson combination pumper and hose truck of 600 gallons and a Reo combination chemical and hose truck. There is a stucco dwelling and a wood shed in block 16, and a confectionery in a blue building at the bottom left. Champion Avenue crosses the bottom of the sheet on a diagonal beside the tracks of the Atlantic City Railroad (P. & R. Ry), with a small building on the line. The borough line of Collingswood and the West Collingswood Extension, part of Haddon Township, runs along the track. Six-inch and four-inch water pipes run in the streets. The adjoining sheets are 13, 12, 16 and 30.
notes: Champion Avenue still exists beside the rail line, but its modern junctions are not used as control because it is drawn wide and diagonal.
A legend beside the fire department lists its apparatus: an Anderson combination pumper and hose truck of 600 gallons and a Reo combination chemical and hose truck.
Adjoining sheets named in the margins are 13, 12, 16 and 30.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-15.description: Sheet 15 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood covers the northeastern corner of the area in the west of the borough, between Richey Avenue at the top and Comley Avenue at the bottom, with Eldridge Avenue along the left edge and Newton Avenue marked not open along the right. The right third of the sheet is Lake Newton, with its drawn banks, a trolley bridge across it and the boundary between the Borough of Collingswood and the Borough of Oaklyn running down the water. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the left, and the compass rose is in the upper margin. The upper block, number 131, has a row of detached frame dwellings on Eldridge Avenue and three pairs of semi-detached brick-fronted houses on Richey Avenue, with poultry houses behind them. The lower block, number 132, holds a row of dwellings on Eldridge Avenue and the Collingswood Sewerage Company disposal plant to the east, with a pumpwell and digesting tank, a settling tank, filter beds and a well house. Beside the lake bank and across Newton Avenue, the plant's sludge beds are drawn as a large outlined enclosure. Four-inch water pipes are marked in Richey Avenue, Comley Avenue and Eldridge Avenue. The empty blocks outlined at the left and bottom belong to sheets 12, 16 and 20.
notes: Newton Avenue is lettered not open and is Newton Lake Drive in OpenStreetMap; the drawn street lies about 3 m further from Eldridge Avenue than the modern one, so its junctions were placed from the Eldridge Avenue junctions by hand.
Cattel Avenue is Cattell Avenue today.
The Collingswood Sewerage Company disposal plant and the trolley bridge over Lake Newton are the notable features.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-16.description: Sheet 16 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood is the southeast corner of the western area, between Comley Avenue at the top and the Atlantic City Railroad at the bottom, with Eldridge Avenue along the left edge and Newton Avenue marked not open along the right. Taylor Avenue crosses the sheet, and Champion Avenue runs on a curve along the railroad. Lake Newton fills the right part of the sheet with a creek and a branch running into it, crossed by the railroad bridge, and the boundary between the Borough of Collingswood and the Borough of Oaklyn runs up the lake. The sheet is drawn at 50 feet to an inch with north toward the left, and the compass rose is in the upper right. Block 133 has a few dwellings, the offices and sheds of Wm. Stout and Son, coal and wood, with a gasoline tank, and the Sanitary Laundry. Block 134 is nearly all greenhouses of Zimmer the Florist, with a potting house, a boiler house and further dwellings. Between Champion Avenue and the tracks of the Atlantic City Railroad of the Philadelphia and Reading Railway stands a long coal trestle, and a pump and saw house with an electric motor stands near Newton Avenue. At the bottom the borough line separates the Borough of Collingswood from the West Collingswood Extension, part of Haddon Township.
notes: Newton Avenue is lettered not open and is Newton Lake Drive in OpenStreetMap; the drawn street lies about 3 m further from Eldridge Avenue than the modern one, so its junctions were placed from the Eldridge Avenue junctions by hand.
Champion Avenue still exists beside the rail line, but its modern junctions are not used as control because it is drawn wide and curved.
The sheet has only four control points, two of them detected, and is low confidence.
Map, 50 ft.

sheet-17.description: Sheet 17 is a full-page map at 100 feet to an inch in the southwest corner of the Borough of Collingswood, with north toward the upper left. The top strip carries the right-of-way of the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (Pennsylvania R.R.) and, below it, the blocks between Park Avenue and the railroad: blocks 233 and 234, laid out with Merion, Narberth and Wayne Terraces running down the page, and the Victor Radiator Co. plant with its long plastered building on block 232. The Gulf Refining Co. has an office, warehouse and iron tank base on a triangular block 231 beside a proposed siding. Park Avenue runs across the page with small detached frame dwellings on its north side (numbers 101 to 137) and a second row of houses on the south side (numbers 100 to 120). From Park Avenue the old White Horse Pike runs diagonally to the southeast, flanked by Clay, Arlington, Richey and Webster Avenues, which cut the large, mostly empty blocks 223 to 229 into long diagonal shapes. The old location of the White Horse Pike is lettered across block 228, and the pike is crossed by an unnamed street. The few buildings are a large dwelling with outbuildings on block 224, a stuccoed tile dwelling near Webster Avenue, and a short row of frame houses in block 223 along the creek. The lower left is taken by the North Branch of Newton Creek, drawn in blue, which winds through the sheet and carries the boundary line between the Borough of Collingswood and the City of Camden; the top left corner lies within Camden. A compass rose stands on block 230. The sheet joins sheet 25 to the north, sheet 18 to the east and sheet 29 to the south.
notes: Modern Park Avenue and Arlington Avenue keep their names; the Terraces are West Narberth Terrace and West Wayne Terrace, and Webster Avenue is probably the Dwight Avenue of today (junction with West Wayne Terrace and Arlington Avenue matched).
The White Horse Pike was moved after 1922 (the sheet marks its old location); the modern pike and Crescent Boulevard do not follow the drawn streets, so they are not used as control.
Margin labels at the top name Overbrook, Merion, Narberth and Wayne Terraces where they continue north of the railroad onto sheet 25.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-18.description: Sheet 18 is a full-page map at 100 feet to an inch of the west-central part of Collingswood, with north toward the upper left. The top of the sheet is bounded by South Atlantic Avenue, with the railroad corridor beyond it on sheet 25. Park Avenue crosses the upper part of the page, with block 235 and the houses on the north side (numbers 207 to 241) and block 227 with houses on the south side (numbers 200 to 218), cut by Wayne Terrace and Franklin Terrace. Franklin Terrace becomes Franklin Avenue at Webster Avenue and runs southeast. At the upper right Virginia Avenue and Browning Road run diagonally away from Park Avenue past blocks 221 and 222, which are lined with small frame dwellings, some stuccoed, with autos and garages behind. Webster Avenue climbs from the lower left to Franklin Avenue, enclosing the large undeveloped block 220. South of it Jessamine Avenue and Harrison Avenue flank block 220A, a closely built row of tile and stucco houses, several drawn in pink as brick. At the lower left the White Horse Pike crosses the sheet from northwest to southeast between blocks 194 and 138, with houses numbered in the 200s and 300s, a fire alarm box at the pike, and two blue-coloured dwellings. Richey Avenue and McGill Avenue cross the pike at the left and the bottom; the blank left margin belongs to Camden and to sheet 17. A compass rose stands at the right. Water pipes of 6, 8 and 12 inches are drawn in most streets. The sheet joins 25 and 26 to the north, 17 to the west, 19 to the east, 29 to the southwest and 11 to the south.
notes: Webster Avenue is Dwight Avenue today; McGill Avenue is Magill Avenue; Wayne and Franklin Terraces are West Wayne Terrace and West Franklin Avenue; Browning Road is West Browning Road.
Park Avenue crosses Browning Road at an offset that today shows as two junctions about 50 m apart; neither was used as control.
South Atlantic Avenue at the top does not match the modern Atlantic Avenue, which lies north of the railroad, and was left out.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-19.description: Sheet 19 is a full-page map at 100 feet to an inch of the part of Collingswood around Knight Park, drawn turned about 65 degrees so that north points toward the upper left edge of the page. The upper half is taken by Knight Park, an undeveloped tract laid out with dashed carriage drives and ovals, a few small outbuildings and one dwelling near its centre, and a pond drawn in blue at the top. The park is bounded on the northwest by Park Avenue, a long diagonal street, and on the south by Browning Road, which crosses the sheet from the left edge to Collings Avenue on the right. A dash-dot boundary line runs across the park and meets Collings Avenue near the right edge. The built-up part lies below Browning Road. Block 137B, between Browning Road and Virginia Avenue, and blocks 135 and 137A carry rows of frame dwellings numbered in the 300s and 400s, several of brick or stucco and drawn in pink. Harrison Avenue and McGill Avenue run down the left and centre of the page, with Franklin Avenue and Virginia Avenue crossing them. Blocks 2, 2A, 137 and 1 to the south are sparsely built, the largest holding a water tower and steel tower with a pump house and other outbuildings. Grant Avenue runs down the right side, with blocks 136 and 1 of scattered dwellings to its east. The White Horse Pike crosses along the bottom edge. Water pipes of 4, 6, 8 and 12 inches are marked in the streets. The sheet adjoins 26 above, 18 at the left, 20 at the right, 11 below and 21 beyond the park.
notes: McGill Avenue is Magill Avenue today; Browning Road is West Browning Road and Franklin Avenue is West Franklin Avenue.
The sheet is turned: the fitted rotation is about -66 degrees, against about -22 on the other sheets of the atlas.
Knight Park is lettered in widely spaced capitals across the park area.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-20.description: Sheet 20 is a full-page map at 100 feet to an inch of the western edge of Collingswood along Lake Newton, drawn turned about 66 degrees so that north points to the left of the page. Collings Avenue runs down the left side from Everett Avenue and the end of Browning Road at the top, past Franklin Avenue, to the White Horse Pike and Richey Avenue at the bottom. Eldridge Avenue crosses Everett Avenue at the top and again meets the pike and Richey Avenue below. Most of the sheet is open ground: block 187 holds a small cluster of frame outbuildings, tool houses and a dwelling (one drawn pink) beside Collings Avenue, and block 21 above it is empty. At the bottom the White Horse Pike runs east across a bridge over the creek, with a 4 inch water pipe in the roadway, and the only closely built block is block 130 between the pike, Richey Avenue and Newton Avenue, with detached frame dwellings, several stuccoed, numbered 600 to 734 and 715 to 731. Blocks 12 and 15 on either side are blank. The right half is taken by Lake Newton and the creek feeding it, drawn in blue, with a trolley bridge across the lake near the bottom. A dash-dot line down the water marks the boundary between the Borough of Collingswood and the Borough of Oaklyn. A compass rose stands at the top. The sheet adjoins 19 on the left and 21 above, with 12 and 15 below the left half; scale 100 feet to an inch is printed at the right.
notes: The lake name is lettered in two separated parts, Newton along the upper water and Lake across the lower water; read together as Lake Newton as on sheet 21 (medium confidence).
Browning Road is West Browning Road today and Franklin Avenue is West Franklin Avenue; Newton Avenue is not in the current street data.
The sheet is turned: the fitted rotation is about -66 degrees, against about -22 on most sheets of the atlas.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-21.description: Sheet 21 is a full-page map at 100 feet to an inch of the west side of Collingswood between Knight Park and Lake Newton, with north toward the upper left. Collings Avenue runs diagonally from the bottom left to the upper right and divides the open ground of Knight Park from the built-up blocks on its southeast side. The park, at the left and top, is drawn with dashed drives, two connected ponds with small bridges, a pavilion, toilets, a bathhouse and a compass rose. Park Avenue crosses the top of the sheet, and a second Park Avenue runs across the upper right corner. Southeast of Collings Avenue a series of cross streets (Everett, Cambridge, Oxford, Colford and Bettlewood Avenues) is laid out with Eldridge Avenue parallel to Collings. Block 186 holds the Edward C. Knight High School, a large pink brick building, with block 186A, 186B and 185 of detached frame dwellings, some stuccoed, along Collings and Eldridge Avenues and around a short curved street. Sunset Lane and Allen Lane cross block 185, where a small stream with a bridge is drawn. The block between Bettlewood and Park Avenues and Lakeview Avenue at the upper right carries a close row of houses numbered in the 200s and 300s. The lower right is the High School Athletic Field, mostly blank, and the shore of Lake Newton with Lake View Drive, marked private, along its edge. A dash-dot line down the water separates the Borough of Collingswood from the Borough of Oaklyn. The sheet adjoins 26 above, 19 and 22 beside it, and 20 below.
notes: Bettlewood Avenue is Bettlewood Avenue in the current street data; Lake View Drive (private) is Lakeview Drive today.

The word Merrick and the separate word Villa are lettered across block 185 around a curved street lettered only Lane; the curved street's name was not read with confidence (medium confidence for Merrick Villa).
Sunset Lane at Collings Avenue came out 10.7 m from its modern position and was not used as control.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-22-1.description: The main part of sheet 22 covers the south end of Collingswood below Park Avenue, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. At the top it takes in the blocks between Park Avenue and Stokes Avenue from Lakeview Avenue east to Dill Avenue, then the blocks along Linnwood, Belmont and Merrick Avenues between Dayton Avenue, Lees Avenue and Lees Lane. Bettlewood Avenue runs diagonally across the lower left toward the shore of Lake Newton. South of Merrick Avenue the blocks thin out into a wedge between the lake and Lees Lane, crossed by two stretches of Mansion Avenue (the western one marked vacated), Chelsea Avenue and the start of Ventnor Avenue at the bottom edge, with Lees Avenue curving south through them. The housing is almost entirely detached frame dwellings of one and a half to two and a half stories with garages and coops behind, thickest along Park, Stokes and Linnwood Avenues and sparse in the lower blocks; a few houses are brick or stucco. Institutions are the First M.E. Church with its Sunday school at Park Avenue and Dayton Avenue, and the Frank M. North Public School near Lees Lane at the upper right. A small stream crosses block 49 to a pool and continues south through blocks 126 and 125 to the lake. The boundary between the Borough of Collingswood and the Borough of Oaklyn runs through Lake Newton at the lower left, and Lees Lane is the line with Haddon Township on the right. Water pipes and hydrants are drawn in most streets. The lower left corner, behind a heavy line, holds a separate inset of block 182 (part 2).
notes: Linnwood Avenue is Linwood Avenue in OpenStreetMap.
The western stretch of Mansion Avenue is lettered (Vacated).
First M.E. Church and Sunday school at Park and Dayton Avenues; Frank M. North Public School at Lees Lane.

Map, 100 ft. South end: Park, Stokes, Linnwood (Linwood), Belmont, Merrick, Mansion, Chelsea, Ventnor Avs; Dayton, Lees Avs, Lees Lane, Dill, Lakeview, Bettlewood Avs; Lake Newton. Two parts: 1 main; 2 inset at lower left behind a heavy line: block 182 south of Ventnor Av at Lees Av (anchored on Lees / Ventnor).

sheet-22-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 22 is an inset in the lower left corner of the sheet, set off by a heavy line and labelled with the sheet number 22. It continues the main part southward beyond the bottom of the page and shows block 182, the southernmost tip of Collingswood, at 100 feet to an inch and at the same orientation as the main map. Ventnor Avenue crosses the top of the inset, with Lees Avenue meeting it from the north between two small corner blocks; south of Ventnor Avenue block 182 narrows to a point between two arms of Lake Newton. The block is empty of buildings: only its outline and one lot line are drawn. The dash-dot boundary between the Borough of Collingswood and the Borough of Oaklyn runs through the lake on both sides of the point, and the lake shore is tinted blue. The inset is placed from a single junction, Lees Avenue and Ventnor Avenue, with the scale and rotation of the main part of the sheet.
notes: Placed from the one junction drawn (Lees Avenue / Ventnor Avenue) with the main part's scale; low confidence.

Map, 100 ft. South end: Park, Stokes, Linnwood (Linwood), Belmont, Merrick, Mansion, Chelsea, Ventnor Avs; Dayton, Lees Avs, Lees Lane, Dill, Lakeview, Bettlewood Avs; Lake Newton. Two parts: 1 main; 2 inset at lower left behind a heavy line: block 182 south of Ventnor Av at Lees Av (anchored on Lees / Ventnor).

sheet-23.description: Sheet 23 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and covers the west side of the borough from Haddon Avenue at the top to Linwood Avenue at the bottom, between Dill Avenue at the left and the Haddon Township line at the right. The West Jersey and Seashore Railroad, shown as a P.R.R. line, crosses the part from left to right with North Atlantic Avenue along its north side and South Atlantic Avenue along its south side. North of the railroad, Homestead, Conrad, Linden, Penn, Ogden and Bryant Avenues rise toward Haddon Avenue and the blocks, numbered 25, 155, 156, 156A, 162 and 162A, hold detached frame dwellings with some brick houses; Haddon Avenue is drawn as a wide street along the top. South of the railroad, Park, Stokes and Linwood Avenues cross Dill, Conrad and Ogden Avenues in a regular grid of blocks numbered 151 to 159, with dense rows of one and two family frame dwellings. Cuthbert Avenue and the borough line run down the right-hand side, and a diagonal line labelled Borough of Collingswood and Haddon Township cuts across the lower right corner, beyond which the sheet is blank. A compass rose and the 100 foot scale bar are printed on the sheet, and 4 and 6 inch water pipes are marked in the streets. Sheets 24 and 22 adjoin above and at the left.
notes: Conrad Avenue is Conard Avenue in OpenStreetMap; North Atlantic Avenue and South Atlantic Avenue are North Atlantic Avenue and Atlantic Avenue.
Linden Avenue north of the railroad is West Linden Avenue; Cuthbert Avenue is now West Cuthbert Boulevard (Haddon Turnpike) and was not used for control.
The sheet is drawn at 100 feet to an inch.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-24.description: Sheet 24 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and covers a wedge of the borough west of the Haddon Township line, between Lawnside Avenue at the upper left and Haddon Avenue along the bottom. The street grid is turned from the northern sheets, so that Haddon Avenue crosses the lower part of the sheet on a slope and Maple Avenue runs across the middle. Oriental Avenue enters from the upper left, bends at East Stiles Avenue and runs east; Homestead, Linden and Penn Avenues run from Oriental Avenue and Maple Avenue down to Haddon Avenue, and Conrad, Linden and Ogden Avenues and Bryant Avenue continue south of Haddon Avenue as short stubs, with Cuthbert Avenue at the lower right. The blocks, numbered 114 to 119 and 161, hold detached frame dwellings of two to two and a half stories on deep lots, with a row of brick dwellings facing Lawnside Avenue along the top and a few brick houses on Maple and Penn Avenues. The diagonal borough line, labelled Borough of Collingswood and Haddon Township, runs from the top to the lower right beside a private lane; the area to its right is blank except for a few scattered buildings at the top. The land left of East Stiles Avenue is blank and belongs to sheet 8. A compass rose and 100 foot scale bar are printed on the sheet. Sheets 10 and 23 adjoin above and below.
notes: Homestead Avenue north of Haddon Avenue is East Homestead Avenue, and the street that continues south of Haddon Avenue as West Homestead Avenue is offset about 15 metres from it; Linden Avenue is East Linden Avenue north of Haddon Avenue.
Conrad Avenue is Conard Avenue today.
The sheet is turned: the grid fits at about -6 degrees.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-25-1.description: The main part of sheet 25 covers the northwest corner of Collingswood at the City of Camden line, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. Haddon Avenue crosses the sheet from left to right, with North Atlantic Avenue, the double track of the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (P.R.R.) and South Atlantic Avenue along the bottom. North of Haddon Avenue the cross streets are Pacific Avenue, Narberth Terrace, Wayne Terrace, Ardmore Avenue, Franklin Avenue and Browning Road at the right edge, with Maple Avenue parallel to Haddon; the blocks north of Maple Avenue (146B to 150B) are laid out but empty, and the open ground beyond runs to the Cooper River at the top. At the left, City Line Road follows the Camden boundary diagonally past Harleigh Cemetery, and a short street lettered Second runs along block 145A. South of Haddon Avenue the streets are Overbrook Terrace, Merion Terrace and Franklin Terrace. The developed frontages face Haddon Avenue: rows of stuccoed and tile dwellings of two and a half stories, many in brick-veneer pairs, with detached frame houses in the blocks behind. The Embury M.E. Church stands on Haddon Avenue in block 148, and Edward Geschke's contractor's storage yard is at the west end of block 145. A heavy line encloses an inset in the upper left corner (part 2) that continues block 145 west of the sheet edge.
notes: Modern names: Narberth, Wayne and Ardmore north of Haddon Avenue are East Narberth Terrace, East Wayne Terrace and East Ardmore Terrace; Franklin Avenue is East Franklin Avenue; North Atlantic Avenue is Atlantic Avenue; Merion Terrace south of Haddon Avenue continues Pacific Avenue.
City Line Road is not in OpenStreetMap; Haddon Avenue at the Camden line is now the Haddon Avenue Approach and Ferry Avenue junction.
East Wayne Terrace / Haddon Avenue was detected 6.8 m off the fit and left out.

Map, 100 ft. Northwest corner at the Camden line: Haddon Av, Maple Av, Pacific, Narberth, Wayne, Ardmore, Franklin Avs, Browning Rd, City Line Rd, N. and S. Atlantic Avs, W.J.&S.R.R.; Cooper River at top. Two parts: 1 main; 2 inset at upper left behind a heavy line: west end of block 145 at City Line Rd, same scale and rotation (placed from one point carried from part 1 at match line A).

sheet-25-2.description: Part 2 of sheet 25 is an inset in the upper left corner of the sheet, enclosed by a heavy line and labelled 25. It continues block 145 of the main part westward beyond the left edge of the page, at the same scale of 100 feet to an inch and the same orientation. Haddon Avenue crosses the top of the inset and City Line Road runs diagonally from it to the southwest along the boundary between the City of Camden and the Borough of Collingswood. Between City Line Road and the dash-dot match line A to B, which joins the inset to the main part, block 145 holds only a dwelling, a coop and a few lot lines. The double track of the West Jersey and Seashore Railroad (P.R.R.) crosses the bottom of the inset. The inset is placed from one point carried from the main part of the sheet, where Haddon Avenue meets the match line, with the main part's scale and rotation.
notes: Placed from one point carried from part 1 (Haddon Avenue at match line A) with the main part's scale and rotation; low confidence.
City Line Road is not in OpenStreetMap; the Haddon Avenue crossing lies at today's Ferry Avenue and Haddon Avenue Approach junction.

Map, 100 ft. Northwest corner at the Camden line: Haddon Av, Maple Av, Pacific, Narberth, Wayne, Ardmore, Franklin Avs, Browning Rd, City Line Rd, N. and S. Atlantic Avs, W.J.&S.R.R.; Cooper River at top. Two parts: 1 main; 2 inset at upper left behind a heavy line: west end of block 145 at City Line Rd, same scale and rotation (placed from one point carried from part 1 at match line A).

sheet-26.description: Sheet 26 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and covers the northwest part of the borough along Haddon Avenue. A narrow strip at the upper right shows the west side of Crestmont Avenue north of Highland Avenue; the rest of the printed area lies below Maple Avenue and runs from Browning Road at the left to Gorman Avenue and Crestmont Avenue at the right. Coulter, Palmer, Summerfield, Hillcrest, East Zane and Garfield Avenues cross the part from Maple Avenue down to Haddon Avenue, which crosses the sheet from left to right. The blocks above Haddon Avenue, numbered 53A to 53E, 102, 175 and 176, hold detached frame dwellings with open lots at the west end, and south of Haddon Avenue the blocks hold a Methodist Episcopal home and the James A. Garfield public school, both drawn in brick, and a pavilion. West Zane and Gorman Avenues continue south to the railroad, shown as P.R.R., with Atlantic Avenue along it, and a row of frame dwellings faces Park Avenue at the bottom, where Browning Road runs in diagonally from the lower left. Wallace Avenue crosses the middle blocks. Most of the upper left of the part is blank. Sheet 25 adjoins at the left, sheet 9 at the upper right and sheets 5 and 1 at the right. A compass rose and scale bar are printed on the sheet; the scan is about five percent larger than the other 100 foot sheets.
notes: Crestmont Avenue is Crestmont Terrace today; Gorman Avenue south of Haddon Avenue is West Gorman Avenue and is offset about 20 metres from Crestmont Avenue.
Coulter, Palmer, Summerfield and Zane Avenues carry East and West prefixes in OpenStreetMap.
The scan is about 4.7 percent larger than the other 100 foot sheets, so the fitted scale is about 4.18 pixels per foot.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-27.description: Sheet 27 covers the open ground at the north edge of Collingswood between the built-up blocks above Highland Avenue and the Cooper River, drawn at 100 feet to an inch with north toward the upper left. Most of the sheet is undeveloped: the Cooper River winds across the upper half in a broad loop, with the boundary between Pensauken Township and the Borough of Collingswood following it, and long tract lines cross the ground below. Development is confined to the bottom of the sheet, where Crestmont Avenue enters from the south with a row of frame dwellings of one and a half to two stories on its west side in block 105A, and Madison Avenue runs parallel to it; the two are joined by a narrow alley. At the right edge Harvard Avenue runs north toward the river, and the plant of the Collingswood Ice Co. stands beside it near the river bank. The sheet adjoins sheet 26 at the lower left, sheet 9 at the bottom and sheet 28 at the right.
notes: Crestmont Avenue is Crestmont Terrace and Madison Avenue is East Madison Avenue today; the alley is Crestmont Lane.
Placed from two hand-picked alley junctions with an assumed scale and rotation; low confidence.
Collingswood Ice Co. on Harvard Avenue near the Cooper River.

Map, 100 ft. Mostly open ground and the Cooper River; Crestmont and Madison Avs joined by an alley (Crestmont Lane) at the bottom, Harvard Av and Collingswood Ice Co. at right. One part, placed from two hand-picked alley junctions with assumed scale and north.

sheet-28.description: Sheet 28 of the July 1922 Sanborn atlas of Collingswood is drawn at 100 feet to an inch and covers the northern edge of the borough along the Cooper River, where several streets run on diagonals across the older grid. Along the left side Harvard Avenue and Woodlawn Terrace run north from Highland Avenue at the bottom, with Princeton Avenue crossing between them, and blocks 29A and 38A hold rows of frame dwellings. Woodlawn Avenue, Lincoln Avenue and Frazer Avenue run diagonally up the page from the lower middle to the right, with Tatem Avenue, King Avenue, Cedar Avenue, Center Avenue, Conger Avenue and Laurel Avenue crossing them in a fan of long narrow blocks, numbered 36, 37, 38, 107 to 110 and 167 to 172. Housing is densest along Woodlawn and Lincoln Avenues, where frame and brick dwellings are drawn on narrow lots, and near the lower middle the William P. Tatem public school stands in brick. A cement block factory and a gasoline engine house are drawn beside Tatem Avenue. The northern blocks are laid out in lots but mostly vacant. The Cooper River winds across the top left, bearing the boundary line between Pensauken Township and the Borough of Collingswood, and a long diagonal line, partly lettered French Lane, marks the borough line with Haddon Township along the upper right. Sheets 27, 6, 7 and 10 adjoin, and a compass rose is printed at the upper right.
notes: The river is lettered Cooper River and the township Pensauken Twp.
The street lettered Center is Center Avenue today; a street segment south of Tatem Avenue is lettered St. (Av.) with the first word not read.
Cedar Avenue, King Avenue and the Princeton Avenue and Washington Avenue junctions with Woodlawn and Lincoln Avenues sit 3 to 14 metres from their modern lines and were left out of the fit.
The street grid fits at about -22 degrees.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-29.description: Sheet 29 is a full-page map at 100 feet to an inch of the southwest part of Collingswood along the North Branch of Newton Creek, drawn turned about 64 degrees so that north points toward the left of the page. The streets form a regular grid on the page. Webster, Harrison and McGill Avenues run down the page, crossed by Richey, Cattell, Comley, Taylor, Sloan and Champion Avenues. The upper blocks, 219 and 139 between Richey and Cattell Avenues, are the most closely built, with rows of detached frame dwellings numbered 204 to 346 and 237 to 341, a greenhouse and many autos and coops. Block 140 below has a few houses and a tool house. Blocks 141 and 142 between Comley and Sloan Avenues are mostly vacant, with a scattering of dwellings along McGill Avenue and a long row of small houses numbered 301 to 329 on the Taylor Avenue side of block 142, two drawn pink as brick. Block 143 has dwellings along Sloan Avenue (numbers 300 to 328). Harrison Avenue is marked not open between Cattell and Comley Avenues and again at the bottom. The left half is taken by the creek, with its dash-dot boundary line separating the Borough of Collingswood from the Borough of Woodlynne and, below the railroad, from the City of Camden. At the bottom Champion Avenue meets the Atlantic City Railroad (Philadelphia and Reading Railway), laid out as a pair of curving tracks. A compass rose stands at the upper left. Adjoining sheets are 17 on the left, 18 above, 11 and 13 to the right.
notes: Webster Avenue is Dwight Avenue today and McGill Avenue is Magill Avenue; Champion Avenue and the lower blocks lie near the modern Crescent Boulevard, which was cut through after 1922.
The creek is lettered Newton Creek with (North Br.) in parentheses at its upper end; North Branch is read from that abbreviation.
Map, 100 ft.

sheet-30.description: Sheet 30 is a full-page map at 100 feet to an inch of West Collingswood, the part of the borough lying in Haddon Township, with north toward the upper right. It is a regular grid of long blocks lettered A to S, bounded on the west by Mount Ephraim Pike, which runs along the City of Camden line, and on the east by Lynne Avenue and the tracks of the Atlantic City Railroad (Haddon Township). Grant, Collings, Eldridge, Elm, Newton, Walnut and Chestnut Avenues cross the page from left to right, intersected by Calvert and Laurel Avenues. The upper blocks, B, C, E, F, H and I, are densely built with detached frame dwellings numbered in the 1100s and 1200s, many with stucco fronts, autos and coops, and a few drawn in pink. Institutions along them are the West Collingswood Presbyterian Church on block C, the Strand Garage and an R.C. Church with a bakery on the western blocks, a public school and a fire department building with its apparatus listed at the right, and the West Collingswood railroad station. At the very top the R. McAllister Coal Yard with trestles and conveyors lies beside the tracks. The lower blocks, M, O, P, R, S and N, are laid out in narrow vacant lots with only a handful of houses. At the bottom Newton Creek crosses the sheet diagonally, with the boundary of Haddon Township and the Borough of Oaklyn running down it; to the right lies the Quaker Cemetery. A compass rose stands at the upper left. The sheet adjoins 13 above the right edge, 14 and 16 to the right and 12 and 15 to the west.
notes: Mount Ephraim Pike is Mount Ephraim Avenue today.
The railroad boundary label at the right reads Boro. of Collingswood; Haddon Township and the City of Camden are named along the top and left boundary lines.
The fitted scale is about 4.04 pixels per foot, 2 percent above the atlas value.
